newsitem.title: USA: Searchers hunt for clues in Miami cargo jet crash.
newsitem.headline: Searchers hunt for clues in Miami cargo jet crash.

text.p: Dozens of investigators combed the charred wreckage of a Fine Air Services Inc. cargo jet near Miami International Airport Friday, hoping to explain the plane's crash and find signs of any more victims.

"The team held an organizational meeting early this morning and investigators are at work as I am speaking to you now," James Hall, chief of the National Transportation Safety Board, told a mid-day news conference near piles of ashy wreckage and charred automobiles left by the crash.

He said 25 investigators, including 15 from the NTSB, were at work on the crash, and said workers at the NTSB's laboratory in Washington, already stretched from this week's air disaster in Guam, had labored through the night examining data from the jet's cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder.

The Fine DC-8-61F aircraft laden with thousands of pounds of fabric had slammed through a busy commercial district adjacent to the airport seconds after takeoff Thursday afternoon, smashing cars, sending up columns of black smoke and scattering flaming wreckage in an accident that aviation officials believe killed all four members of its crew.

But though dozens of small offices near the crash site sustained some damage and remained closed Friday, investigators called it miraculous that there were no immediate reports of deaths or serious injuries on the ground.

"Clearly, it is somewhat of a miracle that the passage of the aircraft stopped short of the buildings, and areas where obviously additional individuals were located and could have been killed," Hall said.

WSVN, the local Fox television affiliate, reported Friday that Renato Alvarez, a 34-year-old Miami resident, had been missing since early Thursday afternoon, when he telephoned his wife at her office near the Fine Air crash site and told her he would be arriving shortly with lunch for both of them.

"I have a feeling that he is there (in the wreckage). I have just this gut feeling that he is there," his wife, Maria Alvarez, told the television station, adding that neither she nor anyone had heard from her husband since the crash.

A Metro-Dade police department spokeswoman said police had had no reports of anyone missing in the crash. And investigators at the crash site said they would have no more information on any survivors until they had spent several more hours on the search.
Sam Williams, assistant director of the Metro-Dade police department, said police teams were charting the crash site into a giant grid, and would spend the day walking over it.
"It's a very lengthy process, it's almost an inch by inch process. We don't want to leave any stone unturned," he said.
The three bodies pulled from the wreckage Thursday had not been identified.

In the wake of the crash, Fine Air announced Friday that it had decided to rescind a recent public offering of its stock, although it said it did not expect the crash would have a material adverse affect on its operations.

As Hall and the other officials spoke with reporters, their news conference was interrupted by shouts of "Smoke, smoke," as a plume of black smoke eerily similar to that from the Fine crash rose next to the airport about a mile from the crash site.
Police raced to the scene, to find a burning, overturned tanker truck. The thick black smoke from the tanker crash forced closure of a runway at Miami International Airport.
